strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and practically relevant gap: existing tree-search decoding methods treat token budget purely as a stopping condition rather than as a variable that should shape search behavior throughout the run.

The proposed BG-MCTS mechanism is a clean, interpretable extension of PUCT-style MCTS: annealing the exploration term by the remaining-budget ratio ρ, adding a depth-based completion bias, and introducing an explicit budget-sensitive widening trigger. The design directly targets the stated failure modes (late over-branching, premature termination).

Experimental coverage is reasonably broad: two open-weight LLMs, two benchmark families (MATH500 Lv.5, AIME24/25), three budget levels, and comparisons against a good range of baselines (parallel sampling, sequential refinement, standard MCTS, AB-MCTS-M, LiteSearch).

The analysis section (answer-reach rate over budget, depth/width trade-off curves, node-level precision statistics, qualitative tree visualizations) provides converging, multi-angle evidence for the intended 'wide-to-deep' behavior, going beyond a single aggregate accuracy table.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: prompts, answer-extraction regexes, hyperparameter search details, and budget-accounting conventions for LiteSearch are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: Benchmark scale is small, especially AIME24/25 (59 problems total, only 2-3 trials averaged), so many reported accuracy differences (e.g., .033 vs .106, or adjacent method deltas of 1-2 questions) may not be statistically distinguishable; no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported despite this being central to the paper's comparative claims.

The ablation study (Table 2) is not fully consistent with the paper's claim that all three components are necessary and complementary: several partial variants match or exceed full BG-MCTS in specific settings (e.g., Explore+Widen without Exploit-shaping reaches .485 at 30K on Llama vs .443 for the full method; Qwen 20K .690 vs .699), undermining the strength of the 'combination is crucial' conclusion.

AB-MCTS-M substantially underperforms simple sampling baselines in this setup, contrary to its original paper; the explanation offered (reward model differences, possible regime mismatch) is speculative and not empirically verified, raising concern about whether the baseline is faithfully tuned/implemented for a fair comparison.

The method's central conditioning variable ρ is a coarse, purely token-count-based proxy for remaining budget; it does not account for problem difficulty, variable per-step generation cost, or how much budget refinement of a given branch actually needs, and no sensitivity analysis is given for the new hyperparameters κ and λ (only c and expansion width are tuned in Appendix B).

The paper's reliance on a single reward model (GenPRM-7B) is acknowledged to produce near-binary/sparse scores, which the authors themselves note weakens search discriminability; since node selection, priors, and the completion bias all depend on Q(x), results could be sensitive to this specific reward model's calibration, and no experiments test robustness to alternative PRMs.

Node-level 'precision' statistics (Table 3/4) that support the 'fewer-trees-but-better-answers' narrative may be confounded: BG-MCTS's late-stage depth concentration mechanically produces answer nodes clustered in high-value subtrees, so higher precision may partly reflect this selection/sampling bias rather than a genuinely stronger quality-per-node signal.

The technical novelty is moderate: the core idea largely amounts to injecting a linear/multiplicative budget-fraction term into existing PUCT exploration and widening-variance formulas; while effective, it is an incremental modification rather than a fundamentally new search paradigm.

strengths: The problem motivation is clear and practically relevant: real-world LLM deployments impose fixed per-query token budgets, and existing tree-search decoders largely treat the budget only as a stopping criterion rather than as a policy-shaping signal.
The proposed BG-PUCT selection rule and budget-guided widening mechanism are conceptually simple, clearly derived from standard PUCT/MCTS, and easy to follow via Algorithm 1.
The empirical evaluation spans two open-weight LLMs, two benchmark families (MATH500, AIME24/25), and three budget levels, giving a reasonably broad (if compute-limited) test bed.

The ablation study (Table 2) isolates the contribution of the three proposed components (explore annealing, exploit shaping, widen annealing), and the qualitative tree visualizations (Figs. 5, 12-15) provide an intuitive illustration of the claimed wide-to-deep behavior.

The additional analyses (answer-reach rate, depth/width trade-off, precision of answered nodes) offer a reasonably thorough attempt to explain *why* the method helps, beyond simply reporting accuracy numbers.
weaknesses: AIME24/25 has a very small number of problems (on the order of 60 combined), so the reported accuracy differences (e.g., .072 vs. .083 vs. .106, or ties such as .156 vs. .156) correspond to only a handful of problems and are unlikely to be statistically meaningful; results are averaged over only 2-3 trials with no reported variance/confidence intervals, undermining the strength of the 'consistently outperforms' claim.

Several baseline results look poorly tuned or under-motivated: AB-MCTS-M underperforms even simple Repeated Sampling in most settings, and the paper's explanation ('may be due to our evaluation setting differing... could become competitive given substantially larger budgets') is speculative rather than empirically verified, raising concern that baselines were not optimized as carefully as BG-MCTS (whose hyperparameters were explicitly grid-searched per Appendix B).

The method introduces several additional heuristic hyperparameters (κ, λ, the depth-bias term, the estimate d̂ans) whose values are fixed by intuition (κ=λ=1) rather than justified theoretically or via sensitivity analysis; only the presence/absence of each mechanism is ablated (Table 2), not the sensitivity to their magnitudes.

The results depend heavily on a specific process reward model (GenPRM-7B) that the authors themselves note produces 'near-binary' and sparse rewards, which they flag as a discussion point but never test with an alternative PRM/reward signal, leaving it unclear whether the reported gains generalize beyond this particular verifier.

The core algorithmic contribution is fundamentally a set of hand-designed annealing schedules (multiplicative ρ factors, (1−ρ) depth-bias) without theoretical grounding or comparison to simpler alternative schedules (e.g., linear vs. other decay forms, or a naive 'switch from wide to deep at 50% budget' heuristic), making it hard to assess whether the specific functional forms chosen are necessary or just one of many workable choices.

The 'fewer-trees-but-better-answers' framing used to explain BG-MCTS's lower tree-level answer-reach rate is a post-hoc rationalization of what could equally be read as a weakness (the method fails to produce any answer for more instances), which is problematic for practical single-response deployment scenarios where an answer must be returned for every query.

Only sub-10B parameter models are evaluated; while resource-constrained settings are a valid motivation, no results with larger/frontier models are shown despite the paper's own Discussion section suggesting relevance to costly API-served frontier models, leaving open whether the wide-to-deep budget-aligned behavior transfers to those settings.

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and practically relevant gap: most tree-search decoding methods treat the token budget only as a stopping condition rather than as a variable that should shape search behavior over time.

The proposed BG-PUCT (budget-annealed exploration term plus depth-biased completion bias) and budget-guided widening (virtual generative child scored by mean/variance with budget-scaled uncertainty bonus) are simple, principled extensions of PUCT-style MCTS that directly target the intended wide-to-deep schedule.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 2 models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B), 2 benchmarks (MATH500 Lv.5, AIME24/25), and 3 budgets (10K/20K/30K), with BG-MCTS winning or tying best in 11/12 settings against multiple competitive baselines (Repeated Sampling, Refinement, AB-MCTS-M, MCTS, LiteSearch).
Thorough ablation study (Table 2) isolating the contribution of each of the three mechanisms, showing they are complementary rather than redundant.

Rich supporting analysis (answer-reach-rate curves, depth/width trade-off plots, node-level precision statistics, and qualitative tree visualizations) that consistently corroborates the claimed 'think first, finish strong' behavior, giving good internal consistency to the story.
Reasonable reproducibility support: algorithm pseudocode, prompt templates, hyperparameter search description, and answer-extraction protocol are all provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Statistical robustness is limited: main results are averaged over only 2–3 trials with no reported variance/confidence intervals, and AIME24/25 has only 30 problems per year (60 total), making single-digit percentage differences (e.g., 0.072 vs 0.083 accuracy) potentially within noise.

The method's effectiveness is demonstrated with a single reward model (GenPRM-7B) that the authors themselves note produces 'near-binary' and poorly calibrated scores; it is unclear how sensitive BG-MCTS's gains are to reward model quality, and no experiments vary the reward model to test robustness of the core claims.

The counter-intuitive underperformance of AB-MCTS-M relative to simple sampling baselines is explained only speculatively ('may be better matched to a frontier-model, higher-compute regime') without further evidence, weakening confidence that baselines were tuned/implemented fairly for this setting.

BG-MCTS introduces several additional hyperparameters (κ, λ, c) beyond standard MCTS; only structural (on/off) ablations are provided, with no sensitivity analysis over their magnitudes, leaving open how much tuning is required for the method to work well in new settings.

Evaluation is restricted to sub-10B open-weight models and math reasoning benchmarks; the significance of the contribution for larger/frontier models or non-math domains (mentioned as motivation in the Discussion, e.g., API-served models) is not empirically tested.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental — it composes known ideas (annealed exploration in PUCT, progressive/dynamic widening, depth-based shaping) under a single budget-ratio conditioning variable, rather than introducing a fundamentally new search paradigm.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and practically relevant gap: existing tree-search decoding methods (MCTS/PUCT variants) treat the token budget purely as a stopping criterion rather than as a variable that should shape search behavior during the process.

The proposed BG-MCTS mechanism is simple and interpretable: annealing the exploration term and adding a depth-based completion bias in the PUCT score (Eq. 3-5), combined with a budget-aware virtual generative child for widening (Eq. 6), together implement an intuitive wide-to-deep schedule.

Experimental coverage is broad: three open-weight LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-32B), two math benchmarks (MATH500 Lv.5, AIME24/25) plus an additional physics benchmark (UGPhysics), and multiple budgets (10K/20K/30K), with consistent improvements over budget-agnostic baselines (MCTS, AB-MCTS-M, LiteSearch, Repeated Sampling, Sequential Refinement).

Extensive ablations and supplementary analyses (component ablation in Table 2, depth/width trade-off analysis, answer-reach-rate analysis, hyperparameter sensitivity sweep, virtual-node ablation, beam-search comparison, interaction with early stopping, PRM score-saturation diagnostics, qualitative tree visualizations) substantially strengthen the empirical case and demonstrate the mechanism behaves as intended.

Honest discussion of limitations, including PRM score saturation and its effect on search granularity, and a thoughtful discussion of implications for data synthesis (coverage vs. precision trade-off).
weaknesses: Statistical robustness is questionable: results are averaged over only 2-3 trials with no variance or confidence intervals reported, and AIME24/25 contains very few problems (typically 30), so several reported accuracy differences (e.g., 0.083 vs 0.089, or improvements of a few percentage points) could plausibly fall within noise, undermining claims of consistent superiority.

Baseline tuning appears asymmetric: a small hyperparameter search was explicitly conducted for the vanilla MCTS baseline (Appendix B), but it is unclear whether comparable tuning effort was applied to AB-MCTS-M and LiteSearch; AB-MCTS-M underperforming even simple Repeated Sampling raises concerns about whether baselines are competitively configured in this specific reward-model regime.

BG-MCTS introduces multiple extra hyperparameters (κ, λ, c, and the ĉ_ans depth estimate) beyond standard PUCT; the hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Appendix G) is only conducted in one setting (MATH500 Lv.5, Qwen2.5-7B, B=20K), leaving open whether the fixed default configuration used in the main experiments transfers robustly across the very different model scales, tasks, and budgets evaluated.

The reward model (GenPRM-7B) used for node evaluation is shown in the appendix to be highly saturated and near-binary, which is acknowledged by the authors as limiting the granularity of the search signal; while this affects all methods equally, it raises questions about whether the reported gains would persist with a more discriminative or differently calibrated reward/verifier, and no experiments with an alternative PRM are provided to test this.

The additional physics evaluation uses a relatively small, non-stratified sample (120 questions across 13 subject areas) and a rollout-based evaluator that is methodologically different from the PRM used in the main experiments, making it a supplementary rather than fully rigorous cross-domain validation.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core contribution is an annealing/scheduling wrapper around existing PUCT-style selection and dynamic widening (both established techniques), rather than a fundamentally new search paradigm; the technical novelty lies mainly in the specific budget-conditioning formulas rather than a new algorithmic principle.

No exploration of substantially different budget regimes (e.g., very small budgets where broad exploration may be infeasible, or very large budgets where the method's advantage may diminish), which would help delineate the boundaries of when budget-conditioning provides the most benefit.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (fixed per-query token budgets in tree-search test-time scaling) that is under-addressed by prior budget-agnostic MCTS variants.

The proposed mechanism (budget-conditioned PUCT annealing, depth-biased completion term, and a virtual generative-child widening trigger) is simple, interpretable, and easy to integrate into standard MCTS/PUCT pipelines.

The empirical evaluation is broad in scope: three open-weight model families/sizes (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-32B), three benchmarks (MATH500, AIME24/25, UGPhysics), and three budgets (10K/20K/30K), plus multiple tree-search and non-tree-search baselines.

Extensive supplementary analysis is provided, including ablations of each component (Table 2), hyperparameter sensitivity (Appendix G), comparisons against beam search and early-stopping variants, and qualitative tree visualizations that intuitively illustrate the intended wide-to-deep behavior.
The discussion section is candid about limitations of the reward model (score saturation) and articulates plausible use cases (budgeted data synthesis) without overselling the results.
weaknesses: Statistical reliability is a serious concern: AIME24/25 has only 30 (or 60 combined) problems, so reported accuracy differences (e.g., .033 vs .039, or .156 vs .156 vs .167) often correspond to a single problem's outcome; results are averaged over only "three trials" (or "two runs" for ablations) with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing reported anywhere in the main text or appendix, making it hard to distinguish genuine improvement from noise.

The AB-MCTS-M baseline underperforms even simple Repeated Sampling in most settings, which is surprising given it is a recent NeurIPS baseline explicitly designed for adaptive branching; the paper's explanation ("mismatch in operating regime... richer feedback and larger compute") is a post-hoc rationalization not substantiated by additional controlled experiments (e.g., re-tuning AB-MCTS-M for this exact regime), raising the possibility that the baseline was not optimally configured, which would inflate the apparent gains of BG-MCTS.

The core technical contribution is a fairly straightforward, heuristic combination of budget-ratio multiplicative annealing (in the exploration bonus), an additive depth-based completion-bias term, and a budget-scaled widening score — the specific functional forms (linear in ρ, division by a running average depth estimate) are not theoretically motivated or compared against alternative parametrizations, so the design feels ad hoc despite empirically reasonable robustness (Appendix G).

The reward model (GenPRM-7B) is reported to be highly saturated/near-binary (Appendix K), which the authors acknowledge limits the granularity of the search signal for all methods; while this is disclosed transparently, it also means the reported gains may partly reflect how well each method copes with a degenerate reward signal rather than genuinely better search under an informative value function, limiting generalizability of the conclusions to more realistic PRMs.

For the UGPhysics evaluation, node evaluation uses n=5 rollouts per non-terminal node to estimate Q(x); it is not made explicit whether the tokens consumed by these rollouts are counted toward the fixed token budget Cused, which is central to the claimed fixed-budget comparison — if rollout tokens are excluded from the budget accounting, the physics results would not be a fair apples-to-apples budget comparison with the main math experiments.

The paper's central quantitative claims rest on tables with many close margins between BG-MCTS and the second-best baseline (e.g., Qwen3-32B AIME 30K: .350 vs .306; MATH500 Qwen2.5 10K: .662 vs .632), and given the lack of variance reporting, it is unclear how many of the "consistent" improvements would survive a more rigorous statistical test, especially on the small AIME24/25 test set.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: existing tree-search decoders (MCTS/PUCT variants) treat the token budget merely as a termination condition rather than as a conditioning variable for search behavior, and the paper articulates concrete failure modes (late-stage over-branching, premature stopping) that this causes.

The proposed BG-PUCT selection rule and budget-guided widening mechanism (virtual generative child) are simple, interpretable extensions of standard PUCT/MCTS that directly target the identified failure modes, and the algorithm (Alg. 1) is clearly specified for reproducibility.

Extensive main experiments across three open-weight LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-32B), two math benchmarks (MATH500 Lv5, AIME24/25), an additional physics benchmark (UGPhysics), and three fixed budgets (10K/20K/30K), with consistent improvements over multiple budget-agnostic baselines (MCTS, AB-MCTS-M, LiteSearch, Repeated Sampling, Refinement).

Thorough ablation of the three core components (Table 2) and an unusually extensive appendix with many additional controlled studies: hyperparameter sensitivity (App. G), effect of the virtual generative node in isolation (App. H), comparison against beam search (App. I), combining BG-MCTS with LiteSearch-style early stopping (App. J), explicit inspection of PRM score saturation (App. K), and detailed data-synthesis implications (App. L) with qualitative tree visualizations (App. M) — this level of due diligence substantially strengthens confidence in the claimed mechanism.

Good complementary analyses (answer-reach rate, node-level precision, depth/width trade-off, qualitative tree diagrams) that directly visualize and corroborate the intended 'wide-to-deep' behavior rather than relying solely on aggregate accuracy numbers.
Honest discussion of limitations, including reward-model score saturation and its effect on search granularity, and directions for future work (input-token accounting, multi-reward-model settings).
weaknesses: Reported accuracies are averaged over only 2–3 trials with no variance/confidence intervals in the main tables, making it difficult to assess whether some of the reported gains (e.g., ties or narrow margins such as AIME24/25 10K for Qwen2.5-7B) are statistically meaningful versus noise, especially on small benchmarks like AIME24/25 (30 questions/year).

The additional physics evaluation uses a small, non-standard subsample (120 questions) and a different, more expensive rollout-based evaluator (n=5 rollouts per node) rather than the PRM used in the main experiments, which limits how directly the physics results can be compared to the math results or generalized as independent confirmation of the method.

The reward model (GenPRM-7B) used for node evaluation is shown in the paper's own analysis (App. K) to produce highly saturated, near-binary scores, which raises the question of how much the method's fine-grained value-based mechanisms (e.g., completion-bias shaping in Eq. 5, mean/variance-based widening score in Eq. 6) are actually being exercised versus effectively degenerating to coarser filtering — the paper acknowledges this but does not test with a better-calibrated reward model to isolate the effect.

The method introduces several additional hyperparameters (κ, λ, c, k) beyond standard MCTS; the sensitivity analysis (App. G) is conducted only in one setting (MATH500 Lv5, Qwen2.5-7B, B=20K) with single runs per configuration, so robustness of the default hyperparameters across models/benchmarks/budgets is not rigorously established.

The design choices for the specific functional forms (linear annealing with ρ, the depth-ratio-based completion bias, mean+variance generative score) are heuristic and motivated by intuition/ablation rather than derived from an optimality argument or theoretical analysis, so it is unclear how sensitive the qualitative benefits are to these particular parametric choices versus alternative budget-conditioning schemes.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonably comprehensive, could be strengthened by including more recent adaptive/budget-aware test-time scaling methods beyond AB-MCTS-M and LiteSearch; the paper's own explanation that AB-MCTS-M underperforms due to an 'operating regime mismatch' suggests possible baseline-tuning sensitivity that is not fully explored.
